overview.text: A double bond is a covalent bond in which two atoms share two pairs of electrons—four electrons altogether. In the usual bonding model, it consists of one sigma (σ) bond and one pi (π) bond. A Lewis structure represents it with two lines, as in C=C, but the two parts differ: the sigma bond forms through head-on orbital overlap, while the pi bond forms through sideways overlap of p orbitals, creating electron density above and below the line between the nuclei. In ethene (C₂H₄), this arrangement helps keep the molecule planar; twisting the atoms would disrupt the pi-bond overlap. A triple bond, by comparison, contains one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

key_facts.text: In a double bond, the shared four electrons occupy one sigma bond and one pi bond.
The sigma bond forms through head-on orbital overlap; the pi bond forms through sideways overlap of p orbitals.
In ethene, the pi bond’s electron density lies above and below the plane of the sigma-bond framework.
Ethene is planar; rotating around its carbon–carbon double bond would disrupt the pi-orbital overlap.
A triple bond has one sigma bond and two pi bonds, distinguishing it from a double bond.
